title: p0-hostedapi-coalescer-tcp-slowstart-congestion-retro-2026-06-30
body:
Summary:

On 2026-06-30 at ~03:42 UTC we observed a large-scale degradation impacting streaming sessions on the Hosted API for ~18 minutes, with elevated TTFB and tail latency and a ~12% increase in 5xx for streaming endpoints. Root cause analysis points to an interaction between the recently deployed edge coalescer optimization, TCP slow-start behavior on certain kernel versions, and an emergent autoscaling gap for edge workers handling high fanout. The coalescer change intended to reduce small-packet overhead by buffering outbound chunks for short windows; under sustained high-concurrency bursts this resulted in synchronized flushes that amplified TCP slow-start congestion across a subset of backend connections, causing persistent queueing and connection stall symptoms.

Severity and Impact:

- Severity: P0 (customer-facing outage affecting latency SLOs and increasing 5xx)
- Impacted surfaces: streaming generate endpoints (HTTP/2 and websockets) across eu-west-1 and us-west-2 regions, affecting ~6% of traffic by token volume during window
- Customer-visible effects: slow initial bytes (TTFB increases from p50 20ms to p50 180ms, p99 > 2s), intermittent stream stalls requiring reconnects, increased timeout-triggered 5xx from gateway timeouts
- Duration: ~03:42 UTC to ~04:00 UTC (root cause mitigations rolled at 03:58 UTC, full recovery and normalization by 04:00 UTC).

Detection and Triage:

- Alerting: the on-call SRE received a P0 streaming-latency alert triggered by p99 streaming latency crossing the threshold and a correlated surge in internal streaming timeouts.
- Initial hypothesis: downstream model inference slowdown or backplane congestion.
- Quick triage findings: model-serving fleet metrics (GPU utilization, request latency within model hosts) were normal. Edge proxy egress queues showed bursts and synchronized flush patterns.
- SRE team pulled packet and connection-level metrics from edge hosts, and traced several sample sessions which showed repeated small-chunk flushes clustering into larger bursts.

Timeline (high level):

- 03:32 UTC: minor increase in streaming session creation rate noted (pilot release from internal app that added fanout).
- 03:42 UTC: automated p99-latency alert fired for streaming endpoints. SRE paged.
- 03:44 UTC: triage ruled out model host issues; edge egress queues and kernel socket retransmit counters elevated.
- 03:48 UTC: hypothesis formed — interaction of coalescer flush window + TCP slow-start causing congestion amplification.
- 03:50 UTC: mitigation plan executed: rollback of the coalescer heuristic (edge-proxy rollback PR merged and rolled to 10% canary -> 50%).
- 03:56 UTC: observed reduction in synchronized flushes on canary hosts, p99 latency decreased.
- 03:58 UTC: full rollback completed across affected edge pools.
- 04:00 UTC: metrics normalized, SLOs restored, page resolved.

Root Cause Analysis:

Primary root cause: The edge coalescer optimization (deployed 2026-06-29) introduced a small buffering window (configurable 4-8ms) that aggregated small application writes into fewer larger packets to reduce syscalls and per-chunk overhead. Under normal loads this improved CPU efficiency and reduced egress packet rate. However, when a sudden high-concurrency fanout event occurred, many connections entered flush cycles aligned to the coalescer window, causing multiple buffered flushes to hit the kernel transmit queue at near-simultaneous moments.

On hosts running Linux kernel 5.19.x with autotuning tcp_autosize engaged, these simultaneous bursts triggered TCP slow-start and congestion avoidance across corresponding peer connections. Because many connections shared constrained NIC ring resources and experienced similar RTTs, the effect amplified: packets were delayed, retransmits increased, and application-level egress queues filled. The coalescer's flush alignment meant the bursts were not spread out, so the usual smoothing that prevents per-packet congestion did not occur.

Contributing factors:

- Autoscaling lag: the edge worker pool scaling policy relies on p95 egress latency and queue depth. The surge was short (minutes) but high-concurrency; autoscaler did not respond fast enough, leaving some hosts with elevated queueing.
- Canary rollout gap: the coalescer change was rolled 100% in production with a single-step deployment across edge pools; no staggered regional canary exposed the problem at lower blast radius.
- Kernel interaction: specific kernel versions with aggressive autotuning made slow-start behavior worse for synchronized bursts. We lacked targeted kernel regression tests in our CI.
- Observability blindspot: we lacked an easy-to-query view correlating application flush timing with socket-level retransmit spikes (we had metrics for both separately, but not aligned traces).

Why prior mitigations didn't prevent outage:
- Circuit breakers and per-connection rate limits are designed for long-lived misbehaving clients; they did not trigger because connections were healthy but flush-synchronized.
- Existing autoscaling thresholds prioritized sustained increases over short instantaneous fanout spikes.

Mitigations and Rollforward Actions Taken:

1) Immediate (during incident):
- Rolled back coalescer heuristic across affected edge pools. Rollback proved effective (observed smoothing of flushes and drop in retransmits within 2–6 minutes).
- Temporarily relaxed gateway timeouts and increased worker queue limits to avoid timeout-triggered 5xx while rollback propagated.

2) Short-term (next 72 hours):
- Reintroduce the coalescer behind a regional canary with 1% traffic for 24h, 5% for next 24h, monitoring socket-level metrics and flush alignment.
- Add a fast-path in edge-proxy: if per-host socket retransmit rate > threshold, disable coalescer locally to avoid creating synchronized bursts.
- Tune autoscaler to consider short-lived burst signals (add a burst-detection metric: sudden delta in concurrent streams over 30s) and scale-out more aggressively for edge worker pools.

3) Long-term (quarter roadmap):
- Add CI tests exercising coalescer under synthetic bursty fanout workloads and multiple kernel versions (5.15–6.1 matrix).
- Invest in socket-level tracing: a new tracing pipeline to correlate app-level write timestamps and kernel TCP events (retransmits, cwnd changes) per-flow for sampled sessions.
- Rework coalescer algorithm to jitter flush windows per-connection to avoid global alignment, and make flush jitter configurable by region and kernel codepath.
- Add canary deployment gating that checks both application and kernel-level metrics before full rollout.

Action Items (owners and ETA):

- SRE/Triage: Create an alert for synchronized flush patterns (metric: fraction of egress writes clusters within 5ms windows) — owner: Ravi Patel — ETA: 2026-07-07
- Edge: Implement local coalescer disable on high-retransmit — owner: Diego Alvarez — ETA: 2026-07-12
- Platform: Autoscaler policy update to add burst-detection signal — owner: Hannah Kim — ETA: 2026-07-09
- Applied ML: Add model-serving smoke checks to rule out model-host contribution for streaming regressions (doc) — owner: Sofia Nguyen — ETA: 2026-07-15
- Observability: Add sampled socket-level trace pipeline and dashboard — owner: Observability Team (linked) — ETA: 2026-08-01
- Delivery: Update rollout guardrails to require regional canaries for edge-proxy heuristics — owner: Release Engineering — ETA: 2026-07-05

Runbook / Playbook Updates:

- Immediate update: Add a section in Hosted API Streaming runbook for "coalescer-induced flush bursts" with quick mitigations (rollback, increase gateway timeouts, temporarily disable coalescer via feature flag).
- New diagnostic steps: how to pull egress write histograms, kernel tcp_retransmits per-socket, and map to application writes (scripts: tools/trace-coalescer).

Lessons Learned:

- Small micro-optimizations at the edge can have macro-level systemic impacts when they interact with kernel networking behavior. Always test across kernel/version matrix and under synthetic bursty fanout workloads.
- Canarying needs to include both application-level and low-level platform signals (kernel, NIC) — surface these signals into deployment gating.
- Autoscalers should consider short, high-amplitude bursts (seconds–minutes) when they cause SLO violations even if not sustained.

Metrics and Evidence Collected:

- Timeline-aligned graphs (attached to Linear ticket LIN-4123): p99 streaming latency, egress write rate, kernel tcp_retransmits, NIC tx_ring_busy, worker queue depth, worker CPU.
- Packet captures from three affected hosts showing clustered write timestamps and corresponding increased retransmit counts.

Open Questions / Follow-ups:

- Should the coalescer be reworked to operate per-stream rather than per-host? (tradeoffs: CPU overhead vs smoothing benefits)
- Are there NIC offload settings (TSO/GSO) interactions we need to consider with coalescer behavior? Plan: schedule hardware-level validation with infra.
- Evaluate whether other recent micro-optimizations could produce similar alignment effects (search PRs since 2026-06-01).

Appendix (short technical notes):

- Edge-proxy PR: github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/981 (coalescer change)
- Rollback PR: github.com/redwood-inference/edge-proxy/pull/984 (rollback/disable flag)
- Incident ticket: LIN-4123
- Kernel versions observed: 5.19.14 (eu-west-1 pool), 5.19.12 (us-west-2 pool), 5.15.x hosts showed milder effect in canary testing.

Post-incident retrospective meeting scheduled: 2026-07-08 15:00 UTC (SRE + Edge + Observability + Release Eng).

Notes to on-call and readers:
- If you encounter a future streaming latency spike, check coalescer flag state first (fastest mitigation), then kernel retransmit metrics, then worker queue depths.
- Keep the rollback play handy and prefer staged canaries for edge heuristics until new jittered algorithm is validated.
